title: Short Stuff: Nose Breathing
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the benefits of nose breathing, prompted by a HowStuffWorks article. Josh shares that he was recently diagnosed with a deviated septum that makes nasal breathing hard. They cite author James Nestor (Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art) on why nasal air is warmed and humidified by the turbinates, how cilia filter particles that get swallowed and digested, and how nasal breathing encourages diaphragmatic breathing and releases nitric oxide, a vasodilator that can lower blood pressure. They describe Dr. John Duillard's 1990s studies showing mouth breathers during exercise had a much higher breathing rate (about 48 vs. 14 breaths per minute) and reported much higher perceived exertion (about 10 vs. 4) at max effort, with similar heart rates. They mention nasal strips popular with athletes, Josh's experience trying to nose breathe while jogging, a study in the journal CHEST (2000) linking nasal breathing to increased lung capacity, and James Nestor's coherent breathing technique of about five to six seconds in and out, with longer exhales suggested for anxiety. They close by saying it's never too late to work on breathing.

segments.title: Opening banter and deviated septum
segments.summary: Josh introduces the topic of nose breathing and shares that he was recently diagnosed with a deviated septum. They joke about nose jobs and 1980s student culture around septum surgery.

segments.title: Why nose breathing: humidification, filtering, and diaphragmatic breathing
segments.summary: James Nestor's view that nasal breathing suits the body. Nasal turbinates warm and humidify air, cilia trap smoke, dander, pollen and mites that are swallowed and digested. Nasal breathing encourages diaphragmatic breathing, which uses the lower lungs where there is more blood.

segments.title: Nitric oxide and blood pressure
segments.summary: Nasal breathing releases nitric oxide, a vasodilator that opens blood vessels, which can lower blood pressure. The hosts say this effect is tied to nasal rather than mouth breathing.

segments.title: Exercise study: breathing rate and perceived exertion
segments.summary: Dr. John Duillard's 1990s studies compared mouth and nose breathers on stationary bikes. Heart rates were similar, but mouth breathers breathed about 48 times per minute versus 14 for nose breathers, and reported exertion around 10 versus 4 at max effort. The hosts also recall nasal strips popular with athletes.

segments.title: Lung capacity and coherent breathing
segments.summary: Josh describes trying to nose breathe while jogging and struggling because of his septum. A CHEST journal study from 2000 is cited as showing nasal breathing can increase lung capacity. Nestor's coherent breathing technique involves about five to six seconds in and out, with longer exhales suggested for anxiety. The hosts mention breathing trainers.

segments.title: Closing thoughts and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts note that breathing and stretching can extend healthy years and that it is never too late to start. They sign off with a note about the show's production company.
